title: Introducing Anyscale GPU Health Observability: From app to hardware | Anyscale
gist: Anyscale launched a private preview of GPU Health Observability that fuses DCGM hardware telemetry (XID errors, ECC counts, NVLink health) with the exact Ray job and node it affects, arguing that owning both the hardware and runtime layers -- something it claims almost no other platform does -- lets it eliminate the manual cross-tool detective work engineers currently do to tell a failing GPU apart from a broken script.

insights.claim: A GPU that is quietly failing looks, from the outside, exactly like a training script that is quietly broken, and Ray currently reports a fatal XID hardware error as a generic worker failure -- sending the engineer to debug the training code instead of the actual hardware fault.
insights.speaker: Mike Tower et al.
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, quantifiable source of wasted engineering time on GPU clusters that this product is designed to eliminate -- a concrete efficiency claim for anyone running large training fleets.
insights.locator: Why we need this level of observability

insights.claim: GPUs can accumulate correctable ECC memory errors for hours, climbing in a metric few people are watching during a large-scale training run, before those errors take a worker down mid-run with no warning.
insights.speaker: Mike Tower et al.
insights.so_what: A leading indicator claim: correctable-error rate is a predictive signal for hardware failure that most teams are not currently monitoring, implying avoidable job restarts today.
insights.locator: Why we need this level of observability

insights.claim: At cluster scale (dozens or hundreds of multi-GPU nodes), a single struggling node simply disappears into the cluster-wide average unless someone happens to manually inspect node by node.
insights.speaker: Mike Tower et al.
insights.locator: Why we need this level of observability

insights.claim: None of the underlying hardware signals are new or secret -- DCGM has reported GPU health data for years and Kubernetes has always emitted pod/scheduling events -- the actual gap has been that this data lives in a different place than the Ray job it affects, requiring a person to manually correlate the two after something has already gone wrong.
insights.speaker: Mike Tower et al.
insights.so_what: Reframes the problem as a correlation/integration gap rather than a data-availability gap, which is the basis for Anyscale's competitive claim below.
insights.locator: Why we need this level of observability

themes.theme: Anyscale's full-stack ownership as a moat

insights.claim: Correlating a hardware signal to the exact job it affected requires a platform to sit at the intersection of the hardware layer and the distributed runtime running on top of it, and Anyscale states that almost no other platform owns both layers simultaneously, which is what lets the correlation happen automatically at the source rather than being manually reconstructed after the fact.
insights.speaker: Mike Tower et al.
insights.so_what: An explicit competitive-moat claim: full-stack ownership (runtime + hardware telemetry) is positioned as structurally hard for point-solution observability vendors to replicate -- worth stress-testing against Datadog, Grafana/Prometheus-based stacks, and NVIDIA's own base station tooling.
insights.locator: Creating a single pane of glass at the source

insights.claim: GPU Health Observability enriches raw DCGM counters (e.g., a bare 'GPU memory used: 38GB' reading) with workload-aware metadata -- the specific job, node, and GPU model -- turning an otherwise meaningless counter into an actionable alert.
insights.speaker: Mike Tower et al.
insights.locator: Creating a single pane of glass at the source

insights.claim: The fleet-level view in the Anyscale console groups every GPU across a customer's entire cloud by node type, Kubernetes cluster, or workload, letting a team running hundreds of GPUs see at a glance which nodes are healthy, degraded, or actively faulting, down to a per-GPU detail panel showing XID code, NVLink replay count, ECC errors, SM clock, and power draw.
insights.speaker: Mike Tower et al.

insights.claim: On the job-level side, when DCGM detects a GPU fault on any node tied to a job, a hardware-error banner automatically appears at the top of the Job Overview page naming the exact node, GPU, and XID error, and the Ray Train view shows which specific worker ranks died on the faulted node versus which completed normally on healthy nodes.
insights.speaker: Mike Tower et al.
insights.so_what: Directly demonstrates the core value proposition -- turning a generic 'worker died' error into an immediately diagnosable, correctly-attributed hardware root cause -- which should reduce mean-time-to-resolution on large training runs.
insights.quote: An Xid 74 (NVLINK_ERROR) error was reported on GPU 3 on node node-gpu-16. This hardware fault may cause this job to fail.

insights.claim: GPU Health Observability is explicitly framed as the first piece of a broader signal layer Anyscale is building out across the rest of 2026, with stated goals of deeper analysis, more granular health signals, and fault tolerance that keeps jobs running even when the underlying hardware is at fault.
insights.speaker: Mike Tower et al.
insights.so_what: Signals Anyscale intends to move beyond passive observability into active fault-tolerant scheduling around hardware degradation -- a roadmap item worth tracking for its potential to reduce GPU-cluster downtime economics broadly.

insights.claim: The same hardware-to-application correlation principle already applies to inference: a recently shipped cluster topology view for Ray Serve maps every deployment, actor, and node into one interactive surface, extending the same reduction in mean-time-to-resolution to the workload type (serving) where uptime matters most.
insights.speaker: Mike Tower et al.
insights.so_what: Indicates Anyscale is building one reusable observability substrate across both training and inference workloads rather than point features, which matters for evaluating platform stickiness.
insights.locator: Beyond jobs and workspaces: the same lens for inference
